plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 1: Structure and Bonding
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a potential energy curve for a pair of hydrogen atoms, drawn on a pale blue field with small green spheres added to show the atomic arrangement at three points along it. A tall gradient arrow at the far left, shaded from cream to orange and labeled Energy, gives the sense of the vertical scale, while the plot's own vertical axis is marked only with a plus sign, a 0, and a minus sign, with a horizontal dashed line drawn across at zero. The horizontal axis is labeled Internuclear distance and ends in a magenta arrow pointing right. One magenta curve drops steeply from the upper left, crosses below zero, reaches a rounded minimum, then rises gradually and levels off toward the zero line at large separation. At the top of the steep branch two green spheres overlap, annotated HH (too close). At the right, two widely separated spheres sit above a magenta dashed line joining the letters H and H, annotated H - - - H (too far). At the bottom of the well two just-touching spheres are labeled H-H, and a short vertical dashed line drops from the minimum to the axis, tagged 74 pm, with a green arrow labeled Bond length pointing to it. The depth and position of the single minimum, read against the two extremes flanking it, mark the separation at which attraction and nuclear repulsion balance and fix the length of a covalent bond.

interactions.label: Internuclear distance (pm)
interactions.teaches: Changing the H-H separation shows that energy is high when atoms are forced too close, lowest at the 74 pm bond length, and approaches zero as atoms become too far apart to bond

Clicking each curve region connects the curve shape to the physical situation: strong repulsion at very short distance, stable bonding at the energy minimum, and essentially no interaction at large separation

demo_steps.title: Too close: repulsion dominates
demo_steps.narration: Drag the atoms very close together. The point climbs the steep left wall of the curve because overlapping electron clouds and nuclei create strong repulsion, raising the potential energy.

demo_steps.title: Bond length: lowest energy
demo_steps.narration: At 74 pm, the point reaches the bottom of the energy well. This is the stable H-H bond length, where attraction between each nucleus and the other atom's electron is balanced by repulsion.

demo_steps.title: Too far: no bond
demo_steps.narration: As the atoms move far apart, the curve rises back toward the zero-energy line. The atoms no longer interact strongly, so there is no stabilizing covalent bond.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Bond length is not arbitrary: it is the distance at the bottom of the potential energy well, where attraction and repulsion balance.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the figure as a qualitative potential-energy diagram on a pale blue background. Use a thick magenta curve with a steep repulsive wall on the left, a clear minimum labeled 74 pm near the lower center-left, and a right tail that asymptotically approaches the dashed zero-energy line. Hydrogen atoms should be green circles with darker outlines; their separation should update with the slider and be paired with a moving marker on the curve. Region clicks should visually emphasize the selected curve segment and the matching atom sketch: overlapping atoms for too close, touching atoms for the bond minimum, separated atoms for too far. Keep the original visual language: green bond-length annotation, magenta distance arrow, dashed zero line, and simple '+ / 0 / −' energy markings rather than numeric y-axis values.

authoredContext:
How close are the two nuclei in the H2 molecule? If they are too close, they will repel each other because both are positively charged. Yet if they’re too far apart, they won’t be able to share the bonding electrons. Thus, there is an optimum distance between nuclei that leads to maximum stability (the figure). Called the bond length, this distance is 74 pm in the H–H molecule. Every covalent bond has both a characteristic bond strength and bond length.

A plot of energy versus internuclear distance for two hydrogen atoms. The distance between nuclei at the minimum energy point is the bond length.

A graph of energy versus internuclear distance. A horizontal line separates the positive and negative energy and a curve with a single trough at 74 ppm is shown.
